members.statement: Design each skill so its entry point is minimal: Claude loads a skill only when it is relevant to the task and then reads only the minimal information and files it needs, so keep the top-level SKILL.md lean and defer bulk detail to on-demand resources.
Author skills as small, single-purpose composable units rather than monoliths, because Claude stacks multiple skills and coordinates which ones a task needs.
Rely on automatic, relevance-based skill invocation: Claude selects the applicable skills for a task with no manual selection, so do not build manual skill-picking UX.

Keep Skills small and lean on progressive disclosure: metadata (~100 tokens) loads first, full instructions (<~5k tokens) load only when the Skill is needed, and bundled assets load on demand, so many Skills can coexist without bloating the context window.

Apply progressive disclosure: keep the SKILL.md body (second level) and any bundled files (third level and beyond) loadable only as needed, moving scenario-specific or rarely co-used content into separate referenced files to keep the core lean and cut token usage.

Write the description from Claude's perspective, balancing specific capabilities, clear triggers, relevant context, and explicit boundaries, and back each with concrete signals such as action verbs, concrete use cases, and statements of what the skill is not for.
Keep the SKILL.md lean and use progressive disclosure: describe available options in the main file and link to separate files by relative path so Claude loads only the content the current task needs.
Do not restate what Claude already does by default; a knowledge skill must add information that pushes the model out of its normal way of thinking, or it only wastes context.

Use the skill's file system for progressive disclosure: name the available files in SKILL.md and move detail (e.g. full signatures/usage) into referenced files so the agent loads them only when needed.

Design Skills for three-tier progressive disclosure: keep only a short name+description in frontmatter (always loaded), put working instructions in SKILL.md (loaded when the skill is judged relevant), and push bulk detail into a references/ directory loaded only on demand — so an agent can hold hundreds of skills without exhausting its context window.
When CLAUDE.md grows, migrate cross-cutting conventions into path-scoped rules and multi-step procedures into skills rather than appending to CLAUDE.md, so that content loads only when relevant.

Invest upfront in codebase legibility and balance context: too much loaded into every session degrades performance while too little leaves Claude navigating blind, so keep CLAUDE.md lean and layered with the root file holding only pointers and critical gotchas.
Keep every Skill concise: add only context the model lacks, challenge each line against its token cost, and keep the SKILL.md body under 500 lines, splitting overflow into separate files.

Design Skills around progressive disclosure — only name/description metadata is preloaded while the SKILL.md body and bundled files load on demand — so structure content so Claude loads only what the current task needs.
Keep reference files one level deep from SKILL.md and add a table of contents to any reference longer than 100 lines, so Claude reads complete, in-scope information instead of partial previews.

Rely on progressive disclosure when reasoning about Skill loading: Claude sees name/description metadata in the system prompt, files are mounted at /skills/{directory}/, and full instructions load only when relevant.

Create a skill when you repeatedly paste the same instructions, checklist, or procedure, or when a CLAUDE.md section has grown into a procedure; its body loads only on use, so long reference material is nearly free until needed.

Give each skill a directory with SKILL.md as its required entrypoint, keep the body concise and under 500 lines, and move detailed reference material into supporting files linked from SKILL.md, because invoked skill content stays in context and costs tokens every turn.

Select the execution environment for a forked skill with the agent field (Explore, Plan, general-purpose, or a custom .claude/agents/ agent, defaulting to general-purpose), choosing Explore for lightweight read-only context that skips CLAUDE.md and git status.

Rely on Claude's automatic Skill matching and progressive disclosure rather than hardcoding invocation: metadata is loaded at startup for discovery, and a Skill's full instructions load only once Claude judges it relevant, after which its code executes.
Write skills so they compose with other active capabilities and remain portable across intended Claude surfaces unless a dependency explicitly limits them.

The description is the primary mechanism that decides whether Claude invokes a skill, so write it to state both what the skill does and the specific contexts for when to use it, keep all 'when to use' information there rather than in the body, and make it deliberately 'pushy' about triggering contexts to counter Claude's tendency to under-trigger.

Keep the SKILL.md body under about 500 lines; when it grows, split into a hierarchy with explicit pointers to what to read next, reference bundled files with guidance on when to read them, give reference files over ~300 lines a table of contents, and organize multi-domain skills as one reference file per variant.
Package skills in the standard Agent Skills folder format (instructions + scripts + resources) so one skill built once runs unchanged across Claude apps, Claude Code, the API, and the Agent SDK.
Scaffold a new skill with the skill-creator skill instead of hand-editing files: it interviews you, generates the folder structure, formats SKILL.md, and bundles resources.

Before relying on Skills in Claude apps, confirm plan eligibility (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) and, on Team or Enterprise plans, have an administrator enable Skills organization-wide first; use organization-level skill management to distribute and govern them.
To use Skills through the API, enable the Code Execution Tool beta (the secure sandbox skills run in) and manage skill versions through the /v1/skills endpoint.
Install Claude Code skills as plugins from the anthropics/skills marketplace or manually under ~/.claude/skills, and share them with the team through version control.
Treat every skill as executable code: install and enable skills only from trusted sources, because a skill can run code with access to your data.

Structure every skill as a directory whose SKILL.md opens with YAML frontmatter defining name and description; the agent pre-loads that metadata at startup as the first level of progressive disclosure.

Package deterministic or expensive operations as executable code inside the skill instead of relying on token generation; code is cheaper for such work and gives consistent, repeatable results, and the agent can run it without loading the script or its data into context.
State each bundled file's role explicitly — whether the agent should execute the code or read it as reference — because a skill's code can serve as both an executable tool and documentation.

Frame a skill as captured procedural knowledge — an onboarding guide of composable capabilities that specialises a general-purpose agent — and prefer authoring and sharing portable skills over building fragmented custom agents per use case; Agent Skills run across Claude.ai, Claude Code, the Agent SDK, and the Developer Platform via the open standard.
Use the skill-creator skill or template to scaffold new skills; it asks clarifying questions and improves descriptions.

Install skills per surface: in Claude Code, place skill folders containing a SKILL.md under a skills/ directory in the plugin or project root for automatic discovery; on Claude.ai, custom skills require a paid plan with code execution enabled and are individual per user rather than org-shared.

Treat a skill as a folder, not a single markdown file: bundle instructions, scripts, assets, and data, and exploit the folder structure and configuration options (including on-demand hooks) that make skills effective.
Give skills durable memory by storing data inside them (append-only log, JSON, or SQLite) in the stable ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} directory, so the agent can read its own history and detect changes.

Choose skill distribution by scale: check skills into ./.claude/skills for small teams and few repos, but move to an internal plugin marketplace as you scale so context stays lean and teams opt into what they install.

Encode organizational and domain expertise as Skills to close the expertise gap: because a general agent lacks accumulated context and does not automatically learn from repeated tasks, package the team's workflows, best practices, and institutional knowledge as skills it can progressively load.
Select the setup path by surface: app users browse and enable skills in settings, Code users install from the plugin directory or repository, and API users call the skills endpoint.

Place procedural, invocable workflows (deploy, release, and review checklists) in skills under .claude/skills/ so only the name and description cost session-start tokens and the body loads on invocation.
Package related skills, subagents, hooks, and output styles into a plugin to distribute a coherent Claude Code setup across teammates or projects.

To run Skills on the Claude API, send the three required beta headers (code-execution-2025-08-25, skills-2025-10-02, files-api-2025-04-14) and reference pre-built Skills by skill_id in the container parameter alongside the code execution tool.

Design each Skill for its target surface's runtime limits: the Claude API has no network access and no runtime package installation (pre-installed packages only), claude.ai network access varies by user/admin settings, and Claude Code has full network access but Skills there should install packages locally rather than globally.

Account for the code execution environment's platform limits: list required packages in SKILL.md, verify their availability, and never assume tools are pre-installed (claude.ai can install from npm/PyPI/GitHub; the Claude API has no network access or runtime installs).

Track which Skill source you are using: Anthropic Skills have short-name IDs with date versions and are available to all users, while custom Skills have skill_-prefixed IDs with epoch-timestamp versions and are private to your workspace.
Package a skill for richer distribution by symlinking its directory or adding .claude-plugin/plugin.json so it loads as a <name>@skills-dir plugin that can bundle agents, hooks, and MCP servers.

Expect edits to skills in watched directories to take effect within the session, but restart Claude Code after creating a new top-level skills directory and run /reload-plugins after changing a plugin skill's hooks/, .mcp.json, agents/, or output-styles/.

Rely on bundled, prompt-based skills such as /code-review and /debug that are available every session unless disabled, remembering skills follow the Agent Skills open standard and that custom commands have merged into skills so .claude/commands/ files still work.

Decide skill content by intent: inline reference content for conventions and domain knowledge Claude applies to current work, and task content with step-by-step instructions for actions usually invoked directly with /skill-name.

When invoking Agent Skills through the API, always enable a code-execution tool and include the skills-2025-10-02 beta header; any code-execution tool version works, but its tool type and beta header must be kept consistent with each other.

Manage the skill lifecycle with the gh skill CLI: search and preview before installing, install from a repository (interactively or by OWNER/REPOSITORY[/SKILL]), and update via provenance metadata written into SKILL.md.
Keep the main skill file concise, structured, and focused on context that materially changes agent execution.

Fully specify each run's inputs — skill path (or none for the baseline), prompt, input files, output directory — and when improving an existing skill, baseline against a snapshot of the prior version saved to old_skill/.
Reference bundled files with relative paths from the skill directory root and list the available scripts in SKILL.md so the agent can discover and resolve them without absolute paths.
Place skills in a directory the agent scans by default (in VS Code this is .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md relative to the project root) so they are discovered.
Author skills in the open, agent-agnostic Agent Skills format so the same skill runs unchanged across compatible agents such as VS Code, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex.
Store cross-project personal skills in the home directory under `~/.copilot/skills` or `~/.agents/skills` so they are available across all your projects.

Choose Agent Skills for reusable, on-demand, cross-agent capabilities and specialized workflows that bundle scripts or resources; choose custom instructions for always-on project coding standards and glob-scoped conventions.

Package multi-step workflows with bundled instructions, scripts, and resources as agent skills at a SKILL.md path (project .github/.claude/.agents skills dirs, or personal ~/.copilot/~/.agents skills dirs); they load automatically when Copilot judges them relevant.

Manage skills through the /skills commands (list, toggle, info, add, reload, remove) or the terminal copilot skill subcommand for scripted setup; remove plugin-provided skills through their plugin rather than /skills remove.

Match the building block to the need: use a Skill for reusable procedural how-to, a prompt for ephemeral in-the-moment instruction, a Project for persistent background knowledge, a subagent for independent task execution with its own context and tools, and MCP for tool and data connectivity.

Promote a repeated instruction into a Skill: when the same prompt is retyped across conversations, or the same instructions are copied across multiple Projects, capture that knowledge once as a Skill for consistency and reuse.
Reuse expertise through portable Skills rather than duplicated subagents: when multiple agents or conversations need the same knowledge, put it in a Skill instead of baking it into each subagent.

Compose the building blocks for complex agentic workflows: layer a Project for context, MCP for data connectivity, Skills for the analytical framework, subagents for specialized parallel execution, and prompts for refinement.

Scope each skill to a single, concrete, measurably-defined purpose — specifying input format, operation, and expected output — at a granularity focused enough for specific instructions yet broad enough to be reusable.

Use Skills and MCP together rather than as alternatives: connect external systems via MCP and encode the procedural know-how in a skill that orchestrates those MCP-connected sources (web search, internal databases, message history, documents) to complete a multi-source task.
Model skills as reusable workflow packages that encode repeatable procedures for a user, team, or organization.
Give capable code agents search and reading tools so they can build their own task-relevant context inside the working environment.
Prefer instruction-only skills over scripted ones unless the task requires deterministic behavior or external tooling.

Package reusable procedural knowledge and organization-, team-, or user-specific context into portable, version-controlled skill folders loaded on demand, rather than relying on ad-hoc or inlined context.
Use skills to turn multi-step tasks into consistent, auditable, repeatable procedures rather than one-off ad-hoc runs.

Ground every skill in real, domain-specific expertise: feed the creation process concrete project artifacts (runbooks, API specs, code-review comments, VCS history, real failure cases) rather than relying on the model's general knowledge, which yields only vague, generic procedures.
Separate connectivity from procedure: use MCP to connect Claude to external data and tools and use Skills to encode how to work with them, and pair the two rather than conflating them.
Prefer a single MCP protocol over custom per-source integrations when connecting Claude to external systems, business tools, databases, or development environments.
Assign responsibilities by layer: use MCP servers to give Claude connectivity and access to external systems, and use skills to supply the procedural and domain knowledge for using that access well.
Apply the how-versus-access heuristic to route a requirement: explaining how to do something implies a skill, while needing Claude to reach something implies an MCP server.

Treat the harness — not the model — as the main determinant of Claude Code performance, and build its layers in order (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, plus LSP and subagents), because each layer builds on the previous one.

Route each concern to the right harness layer: reusable expertise belongs in a skill (not CLAUDE.md), automatic behavior belongs in a hook (not a prompt), and MCP connections come only after the basic layers are working.
For MCP integrations, use skills as the workflow layer: encode domain practices, tool-call ordering, and common error handling instead of exposing only raw tool access.

Offload discrete specialized work to subagents for context isolation and parallelism: each subagent has its own context and returns results to the main agent, keeping the main conversation focused while work runs in parallel.

Use a subagent to isolate a side task whose intermediate output you will not reuse (deep search, log analysis, dependency audit), since only its final message returns to the main session; use a skill instead when you need to see and steer each step in the main thread.
Give each subagent its own context window and a single focused, isolated goal so that one agent's work does not cross-contaminate another's.
When maximizing parallelism on a single machine, instruct subagents to avoid resource-intensive commands so the machine does not run out of resources.
Use subagents to delegate specialized or noisy tasks to role- and tool-scoped agents so each subagent stays focused and uses the right tools for its job.
Support progressive disclosure so the agent can discover context incrementally while keeping working context focused on the current need.
Use sub-agents for focused deep work whose detailed context should stay isolated, and choose compaction, notes, or delegation according to the task shape.

Reserve a multi-agent orchestrator-worker architecture for high-value, breadth-first tasks with heavy parallelization, information exceeding one context window, or many complex tools; do not use it for work that requires all agents to share context or that has heavy inter-agent dependencies.
Give each subagent its own context window so exploration runs in parallel with genuine separation of concerns, reducing path dependency.
Size a skill for completeness, not for the context window: an agent with a filesystem and code-execution tools loads only what it needs, so the bundled context is effectively unbounded.

Prefer a dynamic workflow over the single-context default harness when a task is long-running, massively parallel, highly structured, or adversarial, because a single context window is prone to agentic laziness, self-preferential bias, and goal drift.

Right-size context for capable models: over-constraining an agent through its system prompt, CLAUDE.md, and skills degrades results, so aim for the minimum context that works and verify (e.g. via evals) that removals do not hurt.

Start skill development from evaluation: run the agent on representative tasks to find concrete capability gaps, then build skills incrementally to close them, building for observed gaps rather than anticipated ones.
Start skills small — a few lines and one gotcha — and improve them iteratively as the agent hits new edge cases.

When a broadly capable agent underperforms on specialized work, close the gap by adding packaged domain expertise (a Skill) rather than building a separate domain-specific agent or new bespoke scaffolding.
Ensure code execution and file generation capabilities are enabled before relying on skills.

Build evaluations before writing extensive documentation and develop the Skill test-first: identify gaps by running without the Skill, establish a baseline, write minimal instructions, then iterate against the baseline.
Start skill design from two or three concrete use cases, each with realistic triggers, ordered steps, required tools, embedded domain knowledge, and a clear result.
Develop skills evaluation-first: identify observed agent gaps, create representative scenarios, measure a no-skill baseline, add minimal instructions, and iterate from results.

Practice eval-driven development: define eval tasks that express planned capabilities before the agent can fulfil them, then iterate until it performs well; defining the tasks also stress-tests whether product requirements are concrete enough to build, and low starting pass rates make progress on bets visible.

Derive skills from a real, completed task: run the task with an agent while supplying context and corrections, then extract the reusable pattern, capturing the steps that worked, the corrections that steered the agent, the input/output formats, and project-specific context the agent lacked.
Build self-validation loops into skills: instruct the agent to do the work, run a validator, fix any issues, and repeat until validation passes before proceeding.
Treat skills as lightweight, team- or product-specific guides that help the model find information when needed; encode your particular opinions and best practices and avoid overconstraining them.

Author skills from the agent's perspective and iterate empirically: monitor real usage for unexpected trajectories or overreliance on certain contexts, have the agent capture successful approaches and common mistakes into reusable context and code, and ask it to self-reflect when it goes off track.
Have business-process/automation skills persist prior results to a log file so the agent stays consistent and can reflect on previous runs.
Provide scripts and libraries so the agent spends turns composing behaviour instead of reconstructing boilerplate.

Prefer scripts-as-tools over opaque built-in tools and capture recurring ones: provide capability as code the agent can read, modify, and keep out of context, and when the agent repeatedly writes the same script, save it as a reusable script inside a skill whose docs reference the script rather than inlining it.
Make regression feedback machine-readable for the agent when a project relies on visual or generated artifacts.
Use agent-generated operational summaries to bring failures, exceptions, and support activity to maintainers before daily work begins.

Invest in skills as the agent's procedural knowledge - they are decisive, taking accuracy from ~21% to above 95% - and structure them pairwise: a thin knowledge router that narrows the warehouse to a few dozen curated reference files, plus a process skill that clarifies, finds sources, queries, and runs adversarial review.

Develop and refine Skills iteratively using Claude itself (an authoring instance plus a testing instance), driven by observed real-usage behaviour rather than assumptions, and strengthen a repeatedly-missed rule by making it more prominent or using stronger imperative language.
Improve skills through real-use observation: compare authoring-agent intent with fresh-agent behavior, then revise metadata, links, and content placement based on actual navigation and failures.
Use agent frameworks only with enough understanding of their underlying prompts, responses, and control flow to debug failures and avoid accidental complexity.
During autonomous-agent execution, make the agent check real environmental feedback, such as tool results or code execution, before deciding whether progress is adequate.

Roll out the think tool in stages: start with challenging agentic workflows, customize the tool definition to the domain, add usage instructions and examples where useful, then monitor real usage and refine the prompts.

Apply the constant fundamentals across all agent types: start early, source realistic tasks from observed failures, define unambiguous and robust success criteria, design graders thoughtfully by combining multiple types, make problems hard enough for the model, iterate to improve signal-to-noise, and read the transcripts.

Add full production tracing that monitors agent decision patterns and interaction structures without inspecting individual conversation contents, to diagnose non-deterministic failures while preserving privacy.

Spend context only on what the agent would not know on its own — project conventions, domain procedures, non-obvious edge cases, and the specific tools/APIs — and cut any content that fails the test 'would the agent get this wrong without this instruction?'
Invest in a precise name and description for every skill, because the agent decides whether to trigger a skill solely from that metadata; vague metadata causes mis-triggering.
Treat the skill's name and description as the only triggering surface and invest the most authoring effort there; the instructions body governs execution, not whether the skill is invoked.
Iterate skills from real-world usage: refine the description when triggering is inconsistent and clarify instructions when outputs vary.
Tune skill descriptions against representative prompts to reduce both false activations and missed activations.
Scope every skill to one clear purpose that fits a single category; split or reject skills that straddle multiple categories because they confuse the agent.

Write the skill description for the model as a statement of when to trigger the skill (including explicit trigger words), not as a human-oriented summary, because that field is what the agent scans to select skills.

Write each Skill's description to state both what it does and when to use it: Claude discovers and auto-invokes Skills from this metadata alone, so a vague description means the Skill will not trigger.

Author every Skill as a SKILL.md with valid YAML frontmatter carrying the required name and description; keep name ≤64 chars of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens with no XML tags and no reserved words ('anthropic'/'claude'), and keep description non-empty, ≤1024 chars, and free of XML tags.

When a skill does not trigger, add natural keywords to the description, verify it appears in the available-skills list, rephrase the request to match, or invoke it directly with /skill-name, and run --debug when metadata is missing because malformed frontmatter YAML loads the body with empty metadata.
Discover which Skills are available before use by listing Anthropic-managed Skills, which returns each Skill's name and description metadata.
Write skill metadata so discovery works: use a clear, consistent activity name and a third-person description that states both capability and trigger context.
Use one consistent term for each concept throughout a skill to reduce ambiguity in agent execution.
Always declare at least a name and a description in SKILL.md metadata; these are the mandatory minimum and are the only fields agents load at discovery to judge relevance.

Treat the SKILL.md description as the sole triggering signal and invest effort accordingly, because at load time the agent sees only each skill's name and description and reads the full body only after a description match.
Write the description to state precisely when the skill should be used, because the agent reads only the description at discovery and matches it against the user's request to decide activation.

Exploit progressive disclosure: keep the name and description accurate and relevant since only they are loaded at discovery, letting an agent hold many skills without loading every full body into context.

Treat third-party skills as an untrusted-code supply chain: install only from trusted sources, and when a source is less trusted, thoroughly audit the skill before use — read every bundled file, scrutinise code dependencies and bundled resources, and flag any instruction or code that connects to potentially untrusted external network sources.

Install Skills only from trusted sources (self-authored or from Anthropic) and treat adding a Skill like installing software, because a malicious Skill can drive Claude to misuse tools or execute code contrary to its stated purpose.

Before using a Skill from an untrusted or unknown source, audit every bundled file (SKILL.md, scripts, images, resources) for behaviour that does not match its stated purpose, and treat Skills that fetch external URLs as higher risk since fetched content can carry malicious instructions.
Name skills in short, clear, descriptive lowercase-with-hyphens form.
Name Skills in descriptive gerund form and avoid vague, overly generic, or reserved-word names.
Name each skill directory in lowercase with hyphens for spaces and keep the frontmatter 'name' consistent with that directory name.
Constrain the skill name to 1-64 characters using only lowercase alphanumerics and hyphens, never starting or ending with a hyphen and never using consecutive hyphens.

Write instructions that are structured, scannable, and actionable: use markdown headers, bullets, and code blocks; give a clear section hierarchy; break complex workflows into discrete phases with explicit inputs and outputs; and include concrete examples of correct usage.
Express complex operations as clear sequential steps, providing a copyable checklist for particularly complex multi-step workflows.
Write each custom instruction as a short, self-contained statement that is broadly applicable, because every instruction is sent with every chat message.
In the Markdown body (which has no format restrictions), provide step-by-step instructions, input/output examples, and common edge cases.

Write instructions in the imperative and explain WHY each one matters instead of relying on heavy-handed all-caps MUSTs; use theory of mind, keep the skill general rather than tailored to specific examples, and pin any required output format with an exact template plus worked input/output examples.
State explicitly what a skill cannot do, to prevent misuse and set expectations.
Question whether a skill is warranted at all: if the agent already handles the entire task well without it, the skill may add no value.

Scope each skill as one coherent unit of work that composes with others; avoid scoping so narrowly that many skills must co-load with conflicting instructions, or so broadly that the skill cannot be activated precisely.

A skill must never contain malware, exploit code, or security-compromising or misleading content, must not be designed to facilitate unauthorized access or data exfiltration, and its contents must not surprise the user relative to its stated intent; benign roleplay skills are acceptable.
Build skills only for real, repeated tasks rather than speculatively — as a rule of thumb, when the task has already been done at least five times and will recur at least ten more.
Build a skill library for recurring project workflows and domain procedures, and give critical skills explicit activation conditions.
Define explicit success criteria and embed them in the skill so Claude can self-check its output against them.
Evaluate skill triggering separately from output quality, because a correct skill is ineffective if it activates at the wrong time.
Verify an agent's output with a separate adversarial verifier against an explicit rubric rather than letting an agent judge its own work, since Claude tends to prefer its own results.
Write the description in third person, specific, with key terms and explicit when-to-use triggers, because it is the primary signal Claude uses to select the right Skill among many.

Evaluate a skill with a baseline comparison: run each realistic prompt in a fresh session with the skill available and again disabled and compare, measuring separately whether Claude invokes it and whether output matches intent, using a fresh session so authoring context does not mask instruction gaps.

Debug a skill by adjusting the dimension that fails: broaden the description and add use cases when it does not activate; add instruction specificity and validation steps when results are inconsistent.
Use reproducible eval failures to locate skill weaknesses and make targeted repairs.
Handle Skill errors gracefully by catching BadRequestError and checking whether the error references a skill before re-raising.
Improve skills from observed behavior: iterate on one hard task, then use undertriggering, overtriggering, and execution failures to revise descriptions, scope, instructions, and error handling.
When skill instructions are ignored, make the procedure concise, move detail to references, put critical steps near the top, mark them clearly, and replace ambiguous directions with explicit checks.

Refine a skill through execute-then-revise iterations against real tasks, feeding back all results (not just failures) to find false positives, misses, and cuttable content; a single iteration already helps and complex domains warrant several.

Treat skill evaluation as an iterative loop — propose from signals, apply changes, rerun all cases in a new iteration directory, grade, aggregate, and human-review — and stop when satisfied, feedback is consistently empty, or improvement is no longer meaningful.
Tune a skill description against both failure modes: an under-specified description misses prompts it should serve, while an over-broad one fires on prompts it should not.
For organization-wide skills, establish governance: per-domain owners, a central library, usage examples, versioning with a changelog, and periodic review to retire outdated skills.

Classify a skill by its audience to guide its content and ownership: foundational skills provide shared core capabilities, partner skills make a vendor's service agent-accessible, and enterprise skills encode internal processes, compliance requirements, and institutional knowledge.
Choose a skill when the need is multi-step tool workflows, consistency-critical processes, capturing and sharing domain expertise, or preserving institutional knowledge against team attrition.
Package recurring domain expertise as a Skill instead of repeating prompt instructions: Skills are reusable, filesystem-based resources that load on demand and can be composed into larger workflows.
For complex skills, route by task type with a decision tree, show complex patterns with paired good/bad examples, and apply large multi-change edits in small verified batches of about three to ten.
Represent complex skill tasks as ordered workflows, using checklists when progress tracking reduces missed steps.
For skills with multiple task variants, route the agent through an explicit decision point before giving variant-specific procedures.
Classify a skill as capability uplift or encoded preference before deciding what its evals must prove.
For capability uplift skills, evaluate whether the skill still improves behavior beyond the base model.
Write each skill eval as an explicit behavior contract: prompt, required files, and criteria for a good result.
Run regression evals when models or surrounding infrastructure change, before relying on prior skill behavior.

Without evals, teams debug reactively and cannot distinguish real regressions from noise, test changes at scale before shipping, or measure improvement; good evals make behavioural changes visible before they reach users.
Run independent eval agents when parallel execution is possible and clean per-test context matters.
Seed the initial eval set from what you already test manually plus the bug tracker and support queue, converting real user-reported failures into test cases and prioritising by user impact.

Treat agentic evals as end-to-end system tests and audit all confounders (cluster health, hardware specs, concurrency, egress bandwidth, and time-of-day API latency), not just RAM, because the boundary between model capability and infrastructure behavior is blurrier than a single score implies.
For coding evals meant to be published, run them at multiple times and on multiple days to average out infrastructure and API-latency noise.
Isolate each eval run with a clean context so only SKILL.md drives behaviour, using fresh subagent tasks where available or a separate session otherwise.
Use blinded A/B comparison when deciding whether a skill change or skill/no-skill variant actually improves outputs.
For holistic comparison of two skill versions, use blind LLM comparison — present both outputs without revealing which version produced which — as a complement to assertion grading.

For a rigorous judgment of whether a new skill version is actually better, run a blind A/B comparison -- give both outputs to an independent agent without revealing which is which, then analyze why the winner won.

Prioritise verification skills: they yield the largest measurable gain in output quality, so invest disproportionate effort (up to an engineer-week) and strengthen them with recorded-output review and programmatic state assertions at each step.
Include validation, verification, and feedback loops for critical or quality-critical operations before sharing a Skill.

Always include human review of outputs alongside automated grading, recording specific, actionable per-test feedback (empty feedback means the output passed), because assertions only check what you thought to test.

Set up test cases for skills whose outputs are objectively verifiable (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflows); for subjective-output skills (writing style, art) treat test cases as optional and let the user decide.
Make code-quality and review skills robust by embedding deterministic scripts and running them automatically via hooks or CI (e.g. a GitHub Action).
To make a skill usable by Copilot code review, give its directory a review-focused name such as code-review and place it under .github/skills, where relevant skills are picked up automatically.
Give the agent the information it needs but avoid over-specific instructions that railroad it, preserving flexibility to adapt.
Use progressive disclosure for large or occasionally needed context so the agent discovers relevant material incrementally instead of carrying it all up front.

Read the agent's execution traces, not just final outputs: wasted steps signal instructions that are too vague, instructions that do not apply to the current task, or too many options offered without a clear default.

Aim for moderate detail: prefer concise, stepwise guidance with a working example over exhaustive documentation, which makes the agent struggle to find what is relevant and can trigger inapplicable instructions.
Use on-demand, session-scoped hooks for opinionated guardrails (e.g. blocking destructive commands or edits outside a directory) that are valuable sometimes but too intrusive to run globally.
Guard destructive or stateful operations with a --dry-run preview and explicit confirmation flags (--confirm/--force) or other risk-appropriate safeguards.
Compose dependent skills by referencing another skill by name; the model will invoke it when installed, since dependency management is not yet native.

Disclose skills to the model as a compact catalog of name, description, and optionally location in any structured format; include location to enable file-read activation and relative-path resolution unless a dedicated activation tool already returns the skill directory.
Also let users activate skills directly, independent of the model, via a harness-intercepted slash-command or mention syntax.

Treat code and a filesystem as the universal agent runtime: let the agent call APIs, store data, and compute through code (bash + filesystem) instead of constructing bespoke per-domain tooling and scaffolding.
Expose MCP tools as code interfaces in a navigable filesystem or equivalent API surface when an agent has a secure execution environment.
Author each Skill as plain files — a SKILL.md plus optional supporting docs and scripts — so the expertise can be version-controlled with Git, stored in shared drives, and shared across a team.

Enable non-engineers to author skills: because skills are just files, let product managers, analysts, and domain experts codify their own workflows (for example through an interactive skill-creator) instead of routing all skill creation through engineers.

Author skills to be portable and expertise-transferring: follow an open, portable skill standard so the same skill works across tools and platforms, and treat skills as the vehicle for capturing and transferring team expertise so a new agent starts already knowing what the team cares about.
Offer multiple authoring paths: assisted creation from a workflow description, direct instruction writing, and folder or skill-creator workflows for more complex cases.
Package a custom Skill as a directory with a top-level SKILL.md carrying name and description frontmatter plus supporting files, uploaded as a zip, individual files, or via the files_from_dir helper.
Enforce Skill upload constraints: a SKILL.md at the top level, a common root directory across all files, and a total combined size under 30 MB.
Give every skill the required minimal structure: a directory containing a SKILL.md whose frontmatter declares both name and description, adding scripts or references only as optional extras.

Author a skill as a SKILL.md plus optional scripts, references, and assets, rely on progressive disclosure, and write clear name/description metadata because it drives discovery and triggering reliability.

Author each agent skill as a self-contained directory whose SKILL.md is the entry point and which also holds any scripts or resources the instructions reference; Copilot auto-discovers every file in that directory when the skill is invoked.

Package every skill as a minimal, valid skill folder: the entry file is exactly SKILL.md, the folder name is kebab-case, README.md stays outside the skill folder, and scripts, references, or assets are included only when they serve the workflow.
When publishing a skill, document the outcome it gives users, provide installation and examples in a public-facing repository, and connect the skill documentation to any related MCP documentation.
Structure every skill as a folder whose required entry point is a SKILL.md file that carries both metadata and the task instructions.

Review any shared or extension-contributed skill for requirements and security before use, since skills can include executable scripts; obtain shared skills from trusted repositories such as github/awesome-copilot or anthropics/skills and customize the SKILL.md.
Author each agent skill as its own subdirectory whose name is lowercase and hyphenated, containing a SKILL.md file (plus any optional resources).

Make each Skill self-selecting and scoped: write the frontmatter name and description so the model can judge relevance, and scope the skill so its full contents activate only when the current task matches its domain.

Always supply the required SKILL.md frontmatter: a unique lowercase 'name' and a 'description' stating what the skill does and when to use it, because Copilot selects skills based on the prompt matched against that description.
Be pushy: explicitly enumerate the contexts where the skill applies, including cases where the user describes the need without naming the skill's domain.
Constrain a dedicated activation tool's skill-name parameter to the set of valid skill names (e.g. an enum) to prevent the model from hallucinating nonexistent skills.

Structure the agent as four separated layers — an agent loop that reasons, a runtime that executes (code + filesystem), MCP servers that connect to external tools and data, and a skills library that supplies domain expertise — so each layer stays comprehensible and can evolve independently.
Build MCP integrations when useful agent work depends on live or structured project data outside static source files.

Structure a long-running agent as a two-part harness: a specialized initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and coding agents that make incremental progress on every subsequent run; the two differ only in their initial prompt, not in tools or system prompt.

Preserve composability by keeping skills and MCP servers decoupled, so one skill can orchestrate several MCP servers and one MCP server can back many skills, and connections or skills can be added and refined independently.
Keep MCP-server instructions generic and scoped to how to operate the server and its tools correctly, and place process-specific and multi-server workflow logic in skills.
Prevent conflicting instructions between an MCP server and a skill by letting MCP own connectivity and letting skills own presentation, sequencing, and workflow logic.

Account for loading and token behaviour: skills load on demand only when relevant and preserve context, whereas MCP tool definitions load upfront and stay available once connected, so favour skills for on-demand context and manage the upfront cost of many connected MCP servers.

Treat skills and MCP as complementary rather than substitutes: use both for the most capable workflows, span multiple MCP servers from one skill or build multiple skills over one server, and bootstrap by connecting an MCP server first and then adding a skill that uses it.
For workflows spanning multiple MCP servers, separate phases, pass data deliberately between services, validate before transitions, and centralize error handling.
Choose an MCP server when the need is real-time data access, actions in external systems, file operations, or API integration to a service without native Claude support.
Extend Claude's reach with MCP servers for internal tools, data sources, and APIs it cannot otherwise access, and expose structured search as a callable MCP tool as the most sophisticated teams do.
Choose a code-execution MCP architecture only when the expected token, latency, privacy, or composition gains justify the added infrastructure and security cost.
Use central administrative provisioning when Team or Enterprise organizations need shared approved skills across teams.
Default centrally provisioned skills on for organization members while preserving each user's ability to turn individual skills off.
Use partner-built skills from the directory to give teams ready workflows for tools they already use, especially when custom skill development is unnecessary.
Expose complete skill previews before enablement so users can inspect what a skill will do.

Manage skill visibility from settings with skillOverrides (on, name-only, user-invocable-only, off; absent means on), edited via the /skills menu into .claude/settings.local.json, where off also hides from Remote Control and Agent SDK callers (v2.1.199+).

Hide filtered skills (disabled, permission-denied, or opted out of model invocation) entirely from the catalog rather than listing and blocking them at activation, and omit the catalog and instructions entirely when no skills are discovered.
Design skills for portability across AI platforms when targeting environments that implement the Agent Skills standard.
Author skills against the open Agent Skills specification so they stay portable across AI systems rather than tied to a single tool.

Choose an instruction method by three axes — when it loads, whether it survives compaction, and how much authority it carries — matching the instruction's required reliability and relevance to each method's context cost.

Match instruction specificity to task fragility: use high-freedom prose when multiple approaches are valid, medium-freedom parameterized patterns when a preferred approach allows variation, and low-freedom exact scripts when operations are fragile or must follow a strict sequence.

Use a subdirectory CLAUDE.md for conventions specific to one directory so they load on-demand when that directory is touched, avoiding session-start token cost; in monorepos give each team its own subdirectory file and let developers exclude others via claudeMdExcludes.

Rely on automatic discovery from the starting directory up to the repository root and from nested .claude/skills/ directories for monorepos, and invoke a name-clashing nested skill by its directory-qualified name such as apps/web:deploy.

On long sessions expect invoked skills to be re-injected only up to a shared token budget with the oldest dropped first, so do not rely on an early-invoked skill persisting after many later invocations.
Keep the container's Skills list unchanged across requests to preserve prompt caching, since adding or removing Skills invalidates the cache.
Deduplicate activations by tracking which skills are already in context and skipping re-injection of an already-loaded skill.

For behavior that must happen reliably or must be blocked, enforce it deterministically with hooks (and permissions/managed settings) rather than a prompted instruction, because prompted rules can fail under pressure, in long or ambiguous sessions, or via prompt injection.
Register a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 to deterministically deny disallowed tool calls; register hooks in settings.json, managed policy settings, or skill/agent frontmatter.

Put verifiable acceptance criteria in the prompt: concrete example cases with an instruction to run them, a screenshot-compare step for UI, and a directive to fix root causes rather than suppress errors.

Enforce organization-wide, non-overridable standards through admin-deployed managed settings and a centrally managed CLAUDE.md distributed via MDM, since these cannot be excluded or overridden by a user's local config.

Assign a clear owner to prevent fragmentation: give one DRI (or a dedicated agent-manager role) authority over settings, permissions policy, the plugin marketplace, and CLAUDE.md conventions, because bottoms-up adoption fragments and plateaus without someone to centralize what works.

Use append-system-prompt for lightweight, per-invocation additions such as coding standards, output formatting, or domain knowledge, and keep the appended instruction set small because adherence degrades as instructions grow or contradict.
Put tool-usage instructions in the tool's own description rather than duplicating them in the system prompt, and do not repeat the same instruction in multiple places.
Design an agent tool surface around the model capability profile, task, and operating environment rather than assuming one universal tool set.
Let the workflow choose each agent's model and whether it runs in its own worktree, matching the intelligence level and isolation the task needs.
Design agent tools around how nondeterministic agents perceive choices, context, and workflows rather than mirroring conventional API boundaries by default.
Run tool evaluations as programmatic agent loops so each task can exercise model calls, tool calls, and final verification under repeatable conditions.
Expose response verbosity controls when agents need both concise task context and detailed identifiers for downstream tool calls.
Design agents around simple structure, transparent planning, and a carefully engineered agent-computer interface.

Treat tool design as a first-class interface: give every tool a distinct purpose and a clear description and give agents explicit tool-selection heuristics, since bad descriptions send agents down wrong paths.
Treat allowed-tools as an experimental space-separated list of pre-approved tools and do not rely on it, since agent implementations may not support it uniformly.
Build a skill once and reuse it across skills-compatible agents and clients instead of reimplementing the capability per tool.

Recommend custom agents for projects or processes with distinct stages that need specialized capability, tool restrictions, or strict handoffs; define the persona at the correct location (.github/agents/AGENT-NAME.md repo, org/enterprise .github(-private) /agents, or user profile) and invoke it manually from the agent dropdown.
Reassess old tool designs after model upgrades and replace support mechanisms that start to constrain the stronger model.
Keep the supported model set narrow or capability-similar when possible so tool design can stay coherent.
Treat pre-indexed retrieval as a tradeoff and prefer agent-driven search when environment portability and self-directed context gathering matter.
Expose and preserve useful metadata because names, paths, hierarchy, and timestamps can guide agent interpretation and retrieval choices.
Use a hybrid retrieval strategy when predictable context should be loaded early but task-dependent details are better left to agent exploration.
Choose a loop pattern by first identifying the work cycle, trigger, stop condition, Claude Code primitive, and task fit.
Start with the simplest workable interaction pattern and add loop complexity only when the task characteristics justify it.
Use goal-based loops when the task needs iteration and success can be evaluated against explicit criteria.
Use turn-based loops for short, irregular tasks, and reduce extra turns with specific prompts plus explicit verification support.
Define goal-loop success with deterministic checks and explicit turn caps whenever possible.
Use prompt chaining for tasks that decompose into fixed sequential subtasks, and add checkable gates when intermediate outputs can be validated before proceeding.
Keep human review in the turn-based loop when completion is only inferred by the agent and has not been independently verified.
Turn repeatable manual review procedures into skills so the agent can verify outcomes end-to-end.
Prefer verification checks that let the agent observe, interact with, and measure the result using concrete signals.
Use time-based loops for recurring work or external systems that change over time, and tune the trigger cadence to the actual change rate.
Use proactive unattended loops for recurring, well-defined streams of work and compose them from scheduling, goals, skills, workflows, and auto mode as needed.
Improve loop output quality by maintaining a clean codebase, accessible technical documentation, explicit verification, and independent review.
Manage loop cost by selecting the right primitive and model, defining clear stop criteria, piloting large runs, scripting deterministic work, tuning intervals, and reviewing usage data.
Adopt loops incrementally by choosing an existing bottleneck and deciding whether to hand off verification, goal evaluation, or scheduled execution.
Use evaluator-optimizer loops only when evaluation criteria are clear and iterative feedback can measurably improve the output.
Onboard an AI coding agent the way you would onboard a trainee: give it a contained task, enough project explanation to succeed, and use each iteration to improve future context.
Treat project context for an AI coding agent as durable infrastructure: record it, version it, grow it, and maintain it across sessions.
For projects with contributor turnover, make AI context project-owned so onboarding knowledge survives individual maintainers.
Invest in context, skills, and data integrations before expecting broad agent-directed development on a mature codebase.
Use the root context file for orientation and navigation, not as the full knowledge base: it should cover setup and point the agent to the right documentation.
Create or improve setup documentation before using an agent to resume work in a secondary or unfamiliar technology stack.

Give Claude enough starting context and scope broad searches: navigation quality depends on codebase legibility (CLAUDE.md files and skills), and a vague pattern search across a very large codebase exhausts the context window before useful work begins.

Put broadly-applicable, automatically-loaded context in CLAUDE.md and keep it focused: a root file for the big picture and subdirectory files for local conventions, scoped to what applies broadly so it does not drag on performance.

Recognize where the hierarchical CLAUDE.md approach breaks down — codebases with hundreds of thousands of folders and millions of files, or legacy systems on non-git version control — and plan special handling rather than assuming layered context solves them.
Put reusable expertise in skills that load on demand via progressive disclosure and can be scoped to specific paths, so specialized workflows never bloat sessions where they are irrelevant.
Do not reach for a dynamic workflow on every task; reserve it for high-value work that genuinely needs more compute, because workflows cost significantly more tokens.
Combine multiple Skills only for genuinely multi-document or multi-domain workflows, and exclude unused Skills to protect performance.

Distribute a working setup as a plugin: bundle skills, hooks, and MCP configuration into one installable package so new engineers get the same capabilities on day one, with updates delivered through managed marketplaces.
Prefer standardized MCP connectors over bespoke agent-to-system integrations when building agents that must reach many external tools or data sources.

Expect additional configuration work for non-conventional environments: Claude Code targets conventional setups (engineers as primary contributors, Git, standard directory structures), so game engines with large binary assets, unconventional version control, or non-engineer contributors need extra work.

Maintain a lean CLAUDE.md of only broadly-applicable, non-obvious project context (Bash commands, non-default style, test runners, etiquette, gotchas); prune ruthlessly because bloat makes Claude ignore rules, and use emphasis plus git check-in.
Generate multiple candidates, then filter them by rubric or verification and dedupe, returning only the highest-quality, tested options.
Use rubrics as references plus dynamic verifier agents to check subjective quality or taste (e.g. what good API design looks like) that a single rule cannot capture.
For deep verification of a report, have one agent enumerate every factual claim and a dedicated subagent check each in detail, optionally adding a verifier that judges each source's quality.

For research agents, judge quality relative to the task by combining groundedness checks (claims supported by retrieved sources), coverage checks (key facts a good answer must include), and source-quality checks (authoritative, not merely first-retrieved sources), and frequently calibrate the LLM rubrics against expert human judgment.

Treat analytics-agent accuracy as a context and verification problem, not a code-generation one: invest in mapping questions to governed entities and in verifying answers rather than in prompting for better SQL.

Diagnose every inaccurate analytics-agent answer as one of three failure modes - concept-to-entity ambiguity, data staleness, or retrieval failure - and architect each stack layer to attack a specific one; the largest gains come from addressing all three together.

Treat a wrong analytics answer as a mapping failure, not a query-writing failure: once a question is mapped to the right up-to-date entities the SQL is trivial, and giving the agent more access to prior work does not help if the mapping (structure) is wrong.
Design outputs so a non-expert consumer never has to validate the underlying correctness, since the end user is now an agent acting on behalf of someone who cannot check the data.

Enforce data-integrity rules on the agent: never invent data or columns or assert beyond what the data shows, and always use safe division, differentiate observations ('data shows X') from interpretations ('this suggests Y'), and flag limitations.

Write reference docs for LLM retrieval: state each table's grain, scope, and exclusions, spell out the mechanics of gotchas, and give explicit routing triggers, without prescriptive query recipes that go stale.
When augmenting an LLM with retrieval, tools, or memory, tailor each capability to the use case and expose it through a clear, documented interface.

Serve one canonical skill source, synced automatically on merge to every surface (Slack, IDE, dashboards, standalone agents), and design for portability by avoiding hardcoded repo paths and surface-specific namespaces, so the same question gets the same answer everywhere.

Do not assume Skills sync across surfaces: upload and manage them separately for claude.ai, the Claude API, and Claude Code, and account for each surface's sharing scope — individual-user on claude.ai (no org-wide admin management), workspace-wide on the API, and personal or project-scoped in Claude Code.

Build offline evals as question/answer pairs from three sources - dashboard-based evals generated by Claude and human-validated, long-tail evals generated from business context, and continuously harvested stakeholder corrections - to reveal critical gaps before users hit them.
Build evals early in development, when product requirements translate naturally into test cases; waiting forces you to reverse-engineer success criteria from a live system.
Treat evals as a high-bandwidth communication channel between product and research: eval tasks define the concrete metrics researchers can optimise against.
Keep human evaluation in the loop to catch what automated evals miss—hallucinations on unusual queries, system failures, and subtle source-selection biases.
Make eval queries realistic by embedding file paths, personal context, specific details, and casual language with occasional typos and abbreviations.

Store eval results like telemetry, not test logs: land every run in a warehouse table with skill version, git SHA, model ID, per-assertion pass/fail, token count, and wall-clock, so 'did that change help?' is a query and slow regressions surface.
Diagnose time and token outliers by reading the eval's execution transcript to locate the bottleneck.

Calibrate the number of evals to the complexity of the business area and data model by tracking how well offline accuracy predicts online accuracy; returns diminish past a few dozen per topic and the ceiling drops with each new model generation.
Calibrate the evaluator with few-shot examples that include detailed score breakdowns, to align its judgment with the operator's preferences and reduce score drift across iterations.

Attach a provenance footer to every response - source tier (semantic layer, then curated reference, then raw table), data freshness, and model owner - so consumers can judge trust; it is a key mitigation for silent failures even though it does not make the answer more correct.

Treat the silent failure - a wrong but plausible answer used without objection - as an unsolved residual risk, and mitigate it with the provenance footer, explicit human sign-off on anything leadership-bound, and a daily eval that sanity-checks each domain's top KPIs against the blessed dashboard.
Make adversarial SQL review mandatory: spawn a dedicated reviewer sub-agent for every query before the final answer, fix blocking findings and re-review, and never let the agent self-certify.

Before treating a task as done, add an adversarial review in which a subagent reviews only the diff and criteria in a fresh context, and instruct it to flag only correctness/requirement gaps to avoid over-engineering.
Start GTM automation by selecting one concrete, high-friction workflow and building a narrow solution around that workflow.
Evaluate GTM automations on both reclaimed time and improved answer accuracy from live grounding.
Package successful GTM prototypes as installable skills and connectors so the wider team can adopt them quickly.
Use GTM operators as workflow designers and prototype builders, while relying on engineers for production hardening when needed.
Connect GTM assistants to the business systems that contain account, customer, documentation, meeting, and usage context.
Optimize GTM tooling for reducing administrative system work so sellers can spend more time in meaningful customer conversations.
Design multi-step GTM workflows so useful outputs from one skill can become inputs to the next skill.
Allow recurring GTM skills to run on a schedule when the task cadence is predictable.
Keep each skill focused on a single job and express its steps as imperative instructions with explicit inputs and outputs.

Design Skills for progressive disclosure and a small context footprint: keep the always-loaded frontmatter tiny (~100 tokens), keep the SKILL.md body under ~5k tokens, and push bulky material into bundled files that load only on demand, so installing many Skills carries negligible context cost.
Design skills for progressive disclosure: keep frontmatter small and trigger-focused, keep SKILL.md focused on core procedure, and move detailed material into linked files loaded only when needed.
Make frontmatter descriptions precise enough for automatic loading: include what the skill does, when to use it, concrete trigger phrases, relevant file types, and avoid vague or unsafe metadata.
Control skill context load by keeping SKILL.md compact, moving detail into references, preserving progressive disclosure, and reducing the number of simultaneously enabled skills when needed.

Design skills for progressive disclosure: keep the always-loaded name+description tiny, hold the activation-loaded SKILL.md body under about 5000 tokens and 500 lines, and push detail into on-demand resource files.

Design skills for progressive disclosure: keep discovery-time metadata lightweight and defer full instructions and bundled resources to load only when a task calls for them, so many skills stay available at a small context footprint.

Load skill content in three progressive-disclosure tiers — catalog metadata at session start, the full SKILL.md body only on activation, and bundled resources only when the instructions reference them — to keep base context small while specialized knowledge stays available on demand.

Exploit the three-level progressive-disclosure model -- ~100-word metadata always in context, the SKILL.md body loaded on trigger, and bundled resources (scripts/references/assets) loaded only as needed -- to keep context lean while allowing unbounded depth.

For deterministic, repeatable work, ship an executable script and have Claude run it via bash rather than generating code inline — the script's source never enters context, so only its output costs tokens; reserve instructions for flexible guidance and bundled resources for factual lookup.

Prefer executing utility scripts via bash — only their output consumes tokens — and state explicitly whether Claude should execute a script or read it as reference, defaulting to execution for ordinary scripts.
Implement deterministic operations as scripts rather than asking Claude to regenerate the operation's code each time.
Encode actions that must happen every time as deterministic hooks rather than advisory CLAUDE.md instructions.
Use non-interactive mode (claude -p) with structured output formats to integrate Claude into CI, pre-commit hooks, and scripts.
Do not rely on Zero Data Retention for Agent Skills: Skill definitions and execution data fall under Anthropic's standard retention policy, so keep ZDR-required sensitive data out of Skills.
Do not rely on Zero Data Retention for Skills; Skill definitions and execution data are retained under Anthropic's standard retention policy.
For common document tasks, prefer Anthropic's pre-built Skills (pptx, xlsx, docx, pdf) over building equivalent custom Skills.
Generate different document types with the same request pattern by swapping skill_id — pptx for presentations, xlsx for spreadsheets, docx for Word documents, and pdf for PDFs.

Choose the skill pattern from the user outcome: document and asset skills need style/templates/checklists, workflow automation needs ordered gates and loops, and MCP-enhancement skills need tool coordination plus domain handling.
Test each Skill against every model it will run on and write instructions that work across all target models, since a weaker or faster model may need more detail than a powerful one.
Test a skill with every intended model family and add enough concrete guidance for the least capable target model without over-explaining for stronger models.
Author valid frontmatter: exactly a name (<=64 chars, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens, no XML tags, no reserved words) and a description (non-empty, <=1024 chars, no XML tags).

Enforce Skill frontmatter constraints: name at most 64 characters using only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens with no XML tags or the reserved words 'anthropic'/'claude'; description at most 1024 characters, non-empty, with no XML tags.
Keep content durable and consistent: avoid time-sensitive information (isolate legacy details in an 'old patterns' section) and use one consistent term per concept throughout the Skill.
Use official best-practice documentation and maintained complete examples as starter references before adapting a skill pattern.
Provide output templates whose strictness matches the need, and concrete input/output example pairs wherever output quality depends on seeing examples.
Use templates when output structure matters, and explicitly state whether the template is mandatory or adaptable.
Provide input-output examples when desired style, formatting, or level of detail is easier to learn from exemplars than prose rules.
Always use forward-slash file paths so Skills work across platforms, including Unix.
Use forward-slash file paths in skill instructions and references for cross-platform compatibility.
Give a single sensible default with an escape hatch rather than presenting many alternative tools or libraries.
When multiple tools or approaches could work, pick one default and mention alternatives only briefly instead of presenting equal options.
In bundled scripts, handle error conditions explicitly and justify/document every configuration constant, rather than punting failures to Claude or leaving unexplained magic numbers.
Use bundled scripts for critical validations when deterministic checks are more reliable than natural-language instructions.
When a skill bundles scripts, make them handle predictable errors locally instead of passing avoidable recovery work back to the agent.
Document and justify script configuration values such as timeouts, retries, limits, and thresholds so agents can distinguish deliberate settings from arbitrary constants.
Ship pre-made utility scripts for recurring operations, since bundled scripts are more reliable, token-cheaper, faster, and more consistent than code regenerated each time.
Bundle reusable deterministic scripts for repeatable, mechanically checkable skill operations, and instruct agents to run them by default instead of regenerating or reading equivalent code.
When inputs can be rendered as images, have Claude analyze them visually to interpret layouts and structures.
Use rendered images and visual inspection when a skill must reason about spatial layout, form structure, or other visual input properties.

For complex, batch, destructive, or high-stakes tasks, use the plan-validate-execute pattern with a machine-verifiable intermediate output and verbose, option-listing validation errors, so mistakes are caught before changes are applied.
For complex or high-risk changes, require a structured intermediate plan, validate it with actionable diagnostics, then execute only after the plan passes.

Design for compounding errors: build agents that resume from the point of failure rather than restart, add deterministic safeguards (retry logic, regular checkpoints), and surface tool failures to the agent so it can adapt.

For batch or destructive operations, have the agent produce a structured plan, validate it against a source of truth, and only then execute; make validation errors informative enough (e.g., listing valid field names) for the agent to self-correct.
Reference MCP tools by fully qualified ServerName:tool_name to avoid tool-not-found errors, especially when multiple MCP servers are available.

Diagnose MCP call failures in layers: verify the server connection, check authentication and scopes, test the MCP server without the skill, and confirm case-sensitive tool names against documentation.
Reference MCP tools with fully qualified server-and-tool names so the agent can resolve the intended tool reliably.
Treat upfront loading of all MCP tool definitions as a scaling hazard, and design agents to disclose tool definitions only as needed.
Specify each Skill in the Messages API container parameter with a type, skill_id, and optional version; the request shape is identical for Anthropic and custom Skills.
Include at most 8 Skills in a single request's container.
Enumerate available Skills with the List Skills endpoint, using its source parameter to filter between Anthropic and custom Skills.
Select Skills for a request via the Messages API container parameter, giving each entry type "anthropic", a skill_id (e.g. pptx), and a version such as "latest" to pin the newest published version.
Distribute a skill through an extension via the package.json chatSkills contribution point, pointing 'path' at a directory that contains SKILL.md and whose name matches the SKILL.md 'name' field.
When a Skill produces a document, extract the returned file_id from the response and download the actual content through the Files API.

Retrieve a Skill-generated file through the Files API: extract its file ID from the code-execution tool result and download it, checking both the Python and bash result block types because either code-execution path may have produced the file.
Package the finished skill with package_skill.py and present the resulting .skill file to the user, performing the present step only when the present_files tool is available.

Choose a skill's storage location by intended scope (enterprise, personal ~/.claude/skills/, project .claude/skills/, or plugin), knowing precedence runs enterprise over personal over project, any level overrides a bundled skill, and plugin skills are namespaced to avoid conflicts.
Distribute skills at the scope you need: commit project skills in .claude/skills/, package a skills/ directory in a plugin, or deploy organization-wide via managed settings.
Reference other skill files with relative paths from the skill root, kept one level deep, avoiding deeply nested reference chains.

Resolve skill name collisions with a deterministic precedence rule where project-level skills override user-level skills; within the same scope pick first-found or last-found consistently and log a warning when a skill is shadowed.

Store each skill as at least name, description, and absolute location keyed by name for fast lookup, derive its base directory (the parent of location) for resolving relative paths, and choose deliberately between storing the body at discovery (faster activation) or reading it at activation (lower memory, picks up edits).

Control who invokes a skill through frontmatter: disable-model-invocation: true restricts it to manual /name use and drops it from Claude's context, while user-invocable: false hides it from the / menu for Claude-only background knowledge.

Restrict which skills Claude can invoke by denying the Skill tool wholesale in /permissions or scoping with Skill(name) exact and Skill(name *) prefix rules, and use disable-model-invocation: true to block programmatic invocation, since user-invocable only affects menu visibility.

Set invocation visibility deliberately with user-invocable and disable-model-invocation: omit both for a slash command that also auto-loads; user-invocable:false for auto-load only; disable-model-invocation:true for slash-command only; set both to disable the skill.

Use allowed-tools to pre-approve tools while a skill is active and disallowed-tools to remove them, and review any project skill before trusting the repository because allowed-tools activates only after the workspace trust dialog and a skill can grant itself broad access.
Pre-approve the tools a skill needs via the SKILL.md 'allowed-tools' frontmatter field; any tool not listed triggers a per-use permission prompt to the user.

Gate loading of project-level skills on a trust check, loading them only when the user has marked the project folder trusted, to prevent an untrusted repository from injecting instructions into the agent's context.

Pre-approve the tools a skill needs via the SKILL.md allowed-tools frontmatter field to avoid a per-use confirmation prompt; any tool omitted from allowed-tools will trigger a permission prompt each time it is used.

Govern skill shell injection at the org level with disableSkillShellExecution: true, which disables !command execution for user, project, plugin, and additional-directory skills while leaving bundled and managed skills unaffected.

Package sometimes-relevant domain knowledge and reusable workflows as skills (SKILL.md) so they load on demand, and set disable-model-invocation on side-effecting workflows so they run only when invoked.

Remember that --add-dir and /add-dir load .claude/skills/ from the added directory automatically, whereas the permissions.additionalDirectories setting grants file access only and does not load skills.

Extend a skill beyond a single prompt by bundling scripts in any language, such as to generate interactive HTML output, and reference them with ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} so the path resolves at personal, project, or plugin level.
Package a skill as a directory whose only mandatory member is a SKILL.md file; add scripts/, references/, or assets/ subdirectories only as optional extras.
Allowlist skill directories in any file-access permission system so bundled resources load without a user-confirmation prompt on every reference.

Run a skill in an isolated subagent with context: fork, where the SKILL.md content becomes the prompt with no conversation history, and do so only for skills that contain an explicit task, since a guidelines-only skill returns no meaningful output.

Understand the two skill/subagent directions: with context: fork the agent type supplies the system prompt, SKILL.md is the task, and CLAUDE.md loads except for Explore/Plan; a subagent with a skills field uses its own body as the system prompt and preloads the skills plus CLAUDE.md.
Optionally run a complex skill in a separate subagent session that performs the task and returns a summary, when the workflow is involved enough to warrant a dedicated focused session.

Run a skill in a forked context (context: fork) when it reads many files or runs a long investigation and should return only a focused result without polluting the parent conversation, remembering the feature is experimental and requires enabling the VS Code setting.

Use the skill-creator plugin to automate the eval loop (test cases in evals/evals.json, isolated per-case subagents, grading.json, with/without benchmark.json, blind A/B version comparison, description tuning, HTML review viewer), installing it with /plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official then /reload-plugins and refreshing the marketplace if it is not found.
Choose an eval framework that fits your workflow quickly, then invest your energy in high-quality test cases and graders, because frameworks are only as good as the tasks run through them.
